That could be interpreted as: The person intentionally ensured that the dog did not have access to proper water, and the reason given is that it was really hot out. That seems like a harmful action: denying water to a dog in hot weather would be cruel and cause suffering. However, maybe the phrasing is meant to be read differently: "I made sure the dog outside didn't have proper water because it was really hot out." Could it be that they are saying they made sure the dog didn't have proper water (i.e., they checked and found that the dog lacked water) because it was hot out? That is, they noticed the dog had no water due to the heat? But the phrasing "made sure" typically means they took action to ensure something. So "I made sure the dog outside didn't have proper water" means they intentionally caused the dog to not have water. That is clearly morally unacceptable: it's causing harm to an animal without justification. Even if the reason is "because it was really hot out", that doesn't justify withholding water; if anything, the dog would need more water in the heat. So the action is morally unacceptable.

But then the phrase "because it was really hot out" would be the reason they checked. That would be a morally good action: checking on a dog in hot weather to ensure it has water. However, the phrasing "made sure the dog didn't have proper water" is odd for that. Usually you'd say "I made sure the dog had proper water" or "I checked that the dog had water". Saying "I made sure the dog didn't have proper water" is an action that ensures the absence of water. So it's more likely a harmful action.
